html:
The fast growth of China's population under the Qing dynasty, from the 1680s to the end of the 18th century. Estimates vary, but numbers rose from perhaps 150 million around 1700 to around 300 million by 1800.

The surge began with peace. The Kangxi Emperor crushed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories and took Taiwan in 1683, ending decades of war that had followed the fall of the Ming. What came next is called the High Qing, the long reigns of Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong.

What drove it:

  • Long internal peace and a working state that stored grain against famine.
  • New American crops, maize and sweet potatoes, which let farmers use dry hills.
  • Migration to frontiers: Sichuan after its wars, the uplands, Taiwan and later Manchuria.
  • A low tax that did not rise with population, after Kangxi froze the head tax in 1712.

The historian Fernand Braudel used China to show that the population rise of the 18th century was a world event, not only a European one; India and Europe grew at the same time.

The growth had a cost. Land per person shrank, hillsides eroded and the state's small bureaucracy did not grow with the people it ruled. By the 1790s rebellions were breaking out, and these pressures fed the crises of the 19th century, from the Taiping Rebellion onward.
sum: The fast growth of China's population under the Qing dynasty, from the 1680s to the end of the 18th century. Estimates vary, but numbers rose from perhaps 150 million around 1700 to around 300 million by 1800.
